Enhancing Programming Education: Evaluating the Effectiveness of ITS Agents for First-Year and Advanced Students

Alicia Gates

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2852887                       
  




inf
Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing Lab









Motivation

Programming is an essential skill for many career paths in higher education
~WOS:001289091100374. Despite its importance, many first-year students
find learning to program challenging. Universities often claim that prior
programming knowledge is unnecessary for successfully getting a bachelor's
degree. However, many students struggle with the steep learning curve, and
there is a noticeable gab between those with prior experience and those
without. This presents an additional challenge for
instructors~WOS:001289091100374. In addition, the students-to-instructor
ratio is already high and ever-increasing~WOS:001166861800006. This
makes it very challenging to provide a good personalized learning experience
for all students.

The recent rise in popularity of Large Language Model (LLM) based solutions has
renewed interest in researching learning methods. Intelligent Tutoring Systems
(ITS) have been widely discussed in resent papers, offering personalized and
adaptive learning experiences. They provide feedback and assistance in the
problem-solving process~WOS:001276257200064, including natural language
explanations of code and clarifications for cryptic error messages. The
effectiveness of ITS has been demonstrated in previous
studies~WOS:000345680000001.

Python is a great beginner-friendly programming language and has been
extensively research in the context of teaching with
LLMs~WOS:001166861800006, WOS:001166861800016. Existing research by Brad
Sheese, Mark Liffiton, Jaromir Savelka and Paul
Denny~WOS:001166861800006 focused on a tool designed to assist
undergraduate students in a data science course with their programming tasks.
Their study highlights the tool's capabilities, but it was only tested on
first-year students, leaving a gap in understanding its effectiveness for more
advance students.

An approach to directly provide hints to students is the use of Next-Step
Hints, as explored in research by Lianne Roest, Hieke Keuning and Johan
Jeuring~WOS:001166861800016. Their study showed that generating hints
can be beneficial for students. However, the research lacked a sufficient
sample size, as only three students were questioned. Additionally, concerns
about the quality of the hints were raised. Therefore, I intend to further
explore this issue with a larger student sample size.

The R programming language shares similarities with python. A study from Lukas
Frank, Fabian Herth, Paul Stuwe, Marco Klaiber, Felix Gerschner and Andreas
Theissler~WOS:001289091100374 build upon a Python-centered approach and
improved the method~10.1145/3568812.3603476. I intend to base my
research largely on their approach but focus on Python again. A gap in
their study is the lack of experiments conducted with students.

I intend to build upon these studies by applying their methods to a more
general computer science programming course with a larger participant sample
size. Many studies focus solely on first-year students, but such tools could
also benefit more advanced students. To address this, I will explore the
following research questions:

RQ1: What are the most common challenges students face when getting introduced
to their first year programming experience?

RQ2: How do the challenges for advanced students differ from those of
first-year students?

RQ3: How effective is an ITS agent in providing assistance to both groups of
students?

Approach

I intend to base my work on the study by Lukas Frank, Fabian Herth, Paul Stuwe~
WOS:001289091100374, as it closely aligns with my approach. Their study
evaluated answers from three state-of-the-art (SOTA) models ChatGPT-4,
ChatGPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 using a set of translated R-based questions from Phung
et al~10.1145/3568812.3603476. However, their research did not involve
student participants, which I intend to address.

I plan to build on their methodology by conducting a student-based study and
incorporating the newer ChatGPT-4o models, which were not available at the time.
While they chose R to explore a niche but important language, I will focus on
Python, as it is more widely adopted among both beginner and advanced
programmers. This choice will likely provide a larger participant pool.
Additionally, most studies, including Phung et
al~10.1145/3568812.3603476, focus primarily on first-year students. I
intend to expand on this by including more advanced students.

Another study focusing on hint generation was conducted by Lianne Roest, Hieke
Keuning and Johan Jeuring~WOS:001166861800016. They created a dataset of
step-by-step sequences students followed when solving programming problems and
developed the StAP-Tutor (Step Assistant Programming Tutor) based on this data.
They used prompt engineering to provide students with mostly helpful hints
during problem-solving. While both students and experts generally perceived the
hints as positive, the models sometimes produced unhelpful or misleading
responses. The most notably shortcoming of this study was its small sample
size, as it was based on only three students.

This study gives an opportunity to further explore hint generation with the
aforementioned study. It provides continuous hints to students without
revealing the solution too quickly. However, it is also important to take code
explanations and hints for possibly error into account. Therefore, I plan to
use the first study as a base while incorporating the hint-generation of the
second study.

The third study I found by Brad Sheese, Mark Liffiton, Jaromir Savelka and Paul
Denny~WOS:001166861800006, had a large sample size. They developed a
tutoring system that students could ask during a 12-week period. However, their
study was limited to an introductory data science course. My improvement would
be to expand this approach to include more advanced students as well.

The theory I intend to use involves an ITS agent that students can ask for
hints during problem-solving. This includes explanation of code, errors, and
tasks. Additionally, I plan to include student interview at the end to get
their opinions and potential improvement suggestions.

Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) are designed to imitate human tutors by
providing personalized feedback. They allow students to learn at their own pace
and adapt to individual needs~WOS:001289091100374.

Large language models (LLMs) are deep-learning models trained on enormous
datasets. Their primary function is to generate output, usually text, in
response to user requests called prompts~WOS:001166861800016. These
models can be specifically instructed to respond in a certain way, such as
providing hints instead of solutions or adapting a friendly tone. These
techniques are known as prompt engineering.

The usage of ITS is a popular and proven effective for teaching students,
making it a logical choice. This approach needs to be paired with student
interview to identify and address the key challenges students face.

For this study, I intend to use surveys as a quantitative method and case
studies with follow-up interviews as a qualitative method. My target population
includes first-year students in introductory programming courses and more
advanced students, at least in their third semester. The target sample size for
students should be at least 30. This number is a rough estimate and should be
reevaluated during the student recruitment process. All students should be
bachelor students.

In the beginning I intend to conduct a survey to understand student's
expectations for such a tool. It is important to ask in which year they are and
whether they have prior programming experience. For questions, I intend to use
those from the study of Lukas Frank, Fabian Herth, Paul
Stuwe~WOS:001289091100374, as they consist of simple problems suitable
for first-year students. For more advanced students, I intend to prepare my own
questions. All students should have taken or are in process of visiting an
introductory programming course in a computer science related field.

Using this data, I intend to develop an ITS agent with prompt engineering,
leveraging ChatGPT-4o as this is a current SOTA model (as of 1. December 2024).
I will then conduct a user study where two student groups attempt to solve the
problems using ITS assistance. Students will directly grade the model's
responses on a scale of 1--5, with 1 meaning irrelevant and 5 meaning highly
helpful. Afterward, I will conduct interviews to understand their experiences.
Know with this data on hand and the student's prompt logs, I intend to answer
my research questions.

To conduct this study, I need approval from the university. Especially from the
university's ethics board. Since AI is a relatively new technology certain
potential concerns must be assessed by a third party. One such concern are
biases. The ITS tutor must provide all student with fair and unbiased feedback.
Additionally, students should not become overly reliant on the tutor, and it
should serve as a support tool for teachers rather than a replacement. There is
also the potential for misuse, such as students attempting to obtain direct
answers. Furthermore, students must consent to sharing their prompt logs and
agree to their prompts being processed by the model's provider, raising privacy
concerns.

This study relies on student participation, so a potential challenge is
recruiting enough students. To minimize this risk, I will promote the study
within the university and through university-centered social media.
Additionally, I depend on OpenAI to provide access to ChatGPT-4o, which
requires funding. While the free plan has usage limits, the cost of accessing
the model for the study appears manageable.

This approach also has limitations. Many studies highlight concerns that LLMs
can generate irrelevant or misleading responses, as they tend to hallucinate.
Nevertheless, they have great potential to provide a personalized learning
experience. But, students need to be made aware of these limitations.

To carry out this project, I will need assistance, as the study is expected to
generate a large amount of data requiring human analysis.

The main goal of this study is to research how ITS can help both first-year and
more advanced students with their learning process.

Enhancing Personalized Cancer Treatments Through AI-Driven Analysis of the Tumor Microenvironment
Generative AI in Healthcare
Anita Wong

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2812539                       
  




inf

Motivation
motivation

Cancer remains one of the most complex and devastating diseases, claiming nearly 10 million lives each year globally global_cancer_stats. As we advance into an era of artificial intelligence (AI) and computers being smarter than their creators, AI has emerged as a transformative tool for designing individualized cancer treatment plans. AI-driven systems analyze genetic, imaging, and clinical data to identify optimal therapeutic approaches tailored to each patient indiv_treatment_ai. However, a clear oversight persists: These models often neglect the tumor microenvironment (TME), one of the key determinants of tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment response role_tme. What if AI’s computational power could extend beyond genomic and clinical data to comprehensively decode the TME and adjust treatment plans accordingly?

The tumor microenvironment is a complex ecosystem surrounding a tumor, composed of cancer cells, stromal tissue and the extracellular matrix tme_general. It is a critical yet underutilized frontier in cancer research. It influences how tumors grow, spread, and respond to therapies, making it an essential target for personalized treatment strategies tme_general. Yet, its inherent heterogeneity and multi-dimensional nature make it exceptionally challenging to study using traditional methods. Although machine learning has been applied to other areas of oncology, it has largely overlooked the TME’s complexity and it's impact on tumor growth and development. Existing models for individualized cancer treatment predominantly focus on genomic and molecular tumor markers cancer_targets_ai, leaving TME-specific factors underexplored. This gap hinders the development of therapies that address the full biological landscape of a patient’s cancer.

AI is increasingly recognized in academia and healthcare for its ability to revolutionize oncology by processing complex datasets and uncovering hidden patterns. However, current AI models rarely incorporate the dynamic interplay within the TME, such as immune cell infiltration, stromal interactions, or extracellular signaling pathways tme_ai. This omission limits their precision and applicability in real-world therapeutic settings, where TME factors can significantly alter treatment efficacy.

To bridge this critical research gap, this study will evaluate how integrating TME data into computational models can enhance the accuracy and applicability of treatment predictions.

The research will explore the following key questions:

     How does the heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment impact treatment response predictions?
     What are the limitations of current AI-driven models in incorporating TME data, and how can these be addressed?
     How can integrating TME characteristics improve the predictive accuracy of personalized cancer treatments?

By systematically analyzing these questions, this study aims to refine data analysis methods in oncology, ensuring that treatment models reflect the full biological complexity of each patient’s cancer. The findings will contribute to developing more effective, individualized therapeutic strategies, ultimately advancing precision medicine in oncology.


Approach

State of the Art

AI has advanced oncology by improving genomics-based therapy selection, patient stratification, and biomarker discovery cancer_targets_ai. Deep learning models analyze genomic data to predict treatment responses, yet, as highlighted in the motivation section, they often overlook the tumor microenvironment (TME) role_tme. This dynamic ecosystem of cancer cells, stromal components, and immune infiltrates plays a crucial role in tumor progression and therapy efficacy tme_general, but its complexity remains a challenge for AI-driven analysis tme_ai.

Key limitations in existing cancer treatment plan prediction models include:


     Limited TME Integration: AI models focus on genomic markers, neglecting cancer-TME interactions, reducing prediction accuracy cancer_targets_ai.
     Scalability Challenges: The high-dimensional, heterogeneous TME data is difficult to integrate into traditional machine learning models systems_bio_tme.
     Lack of Personalization: As processing time of TME-data is large due to its heterogenity tme_ai, models often neglect the personalization aspect of cancer treatment predictions when computing cancer_targets_ai, which limits the precision treatment approaches.



Theoretical Framework

The theoretical foundation for this research is built on the interplay between AI-driven data analysis and Systems biology. 

The concepts of Data Science, Semi-supervised and Reinforcement Learning algorithms have already been used to predict individualized treatment plan treatment_plan_pred and complications of brain cancer ss_learning_predictions_cancer. Both research findings hold exceptional potential for advancing the understanding of TME datasets and enhancing the accuracy of personalized treatment plan predictions.

Systems biology defines TME as a dynamic and multi-faceted system where interactions between cancer cells, immune cells and extracellular components drive tumor growth and response to treatment systems_bio_tme. This approach focuses on capturing the cellular heterogeneity, the spatial organization of immune cells, and the interactions between stromal and tumor cells—factors that are critical to understanding cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes systems_bio_tme. These aspects provide the foundation for computational models that can represent the complexity of the TME in a meaningful way.

Methodology

General

As analysing tumor microenvironment is pretty complex and it requires significant compute resources compute_res_analysis, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) goodfellow2014generativeadversarialnetworks will be trained to "compress" essential features of TME into separate datasets for further analysis of TME's impact on personalized cancer treatment. Sequenced tumor microenvironments will be taken from public databases, for example the one of "The Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA)" tcga.

baseline
For developing a unique machine learning model that would consider the TME to predict cancer treatments plans, as a basis we will use a deep learning framework introduced in treatment_plan_pred treatment_plan_pred. The framework predicts cancer treatment plans by integrating imaging and clinical data. It uses a multi-branch architecture, where convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extract features from medical images, while fully connected layers process structured clinical and genomic data. These features are merged to generate treatment predictions, with techniques like attention mechanisms improving interpretability and optimization ensuring clinical relevance.

Testing and Evaluation

The methodology leverages Generative Adversarial Networks for feature compression of the tumor microenvironment (TME) data that is mostly represented by images tme_ai, which is then used as input for the AI model to predict individualized treatment outcomes. Testing this approach involves evaluating both its conceptual soundness and practical effectiveness.

The quality of the GAN's data compression will be assessed using metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM). These metrics will compare the GAN-generated features with the original TME data to determine whether essential biological information is preserved.

The treatment plan predictive model's ability to use GAN-compressed TME data as input will be tested by comparing its predictive accuracy before and after integrating this data. Performance improvements will be measured using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The performance of the AI model using GAN-enhanced TME datasets will be compared to the baseline model introduced above (baseline).

Limitations

While the model’s predictions will be tested against known treatment outcomes, real-world clinical validation is needed to confirm the model’s accuracy and efficacy in guiding actual treatment decisions. This requires extensive collaboration with healthcare professionals and integration with clinical workflows.

The model’s ability to generalize to diverse patient populations is an important concern. The datasets used in training might not fully represent all demographics, potentially limiting the applicability of the model in clinical practice.

Holographic AI Assistants in Museums: Simulating Historical Personalities
Enhance museum experiences by providing real-time, immersive interactions with historical personalities
April Byrd

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2616065                       
  




inf
Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing Lab










Motivation

"The modern museum has multiple purposes - to curate and preserve, to research, and to reach out to the public. They challenge us and ask us to question our assumptions about the past or the world around us." kate_williams This quote by Kate Williams, a renowned British historian, author and television presenter, captures the essence of museums. But especially the part about reaching out to the public doesn't hold truth nowadays. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, museums worldwide have faced a dramatic decline in visitor numbers visitor_2021, highlighting the need for more engaging and innovative approaches to attract audiences.  For example, the National Gallery in London still had a 55\


While some museums already started using holograms, these typically serve as  representation of objects and animals. Holographic AI assistants, trained to emulate historical personalities and reproduce contextual information, could transform the entire museum experience. These assistants provide new and interactive ways for visitors to engage with them and present information based on their interest. 

Research questions:

RQ1 How can holographic AI assistants be trained and implemented in museums to enhance the visitor experience?

	 Sub-RQ1.1 What technical requirements are necessary to model historical personalities in holographic AI assistants, including the use of authentic data sources, large language models and holographic visualization?
	 Sub-RQ1.2 What ethical and data privacy challenges arise from training holographic AI assistants to accurately represent historical personalities in museums?
	 Sub-RQ1.3 How do museum visitors respond to the visual representation and interactivity of holographic AI assistants?


Approach

Digitalization requires museums to implicate new thought provoking and immersive ways to interact with its content. Holographic AI assistants which allow context based communication, might be the solution for enhancing visitor engagement.  They enable dynamic dialogues between visitors and representations of historical personalities, enriching educational experiences and making history more captivating and accessible. Scientific papers already show the use of cutting edge visualization via holograms pietroni_bringing_2019, caggianese_discovering_2020 with additional gesture control and first attempts at implementing AI in museums by providing heritage chatbots caggianese_discovering_2020. This study will analyze the possibility of synergistically combining both holography and AI assistants to enable immersive and historically accurate interactions between museum visitors and virtual personalities.

To understand the need for AI assistants to have a physical presence, especially in museums, it is important to look at how people prefer to engage in deep conversations to gain insights and derive lasting values from them. John Short, Ederyn Williams, and Bruce Christie introduced the social presence theory in 1976 in their book "The Social Psychology of Telecommunications". This theory refers to the perceived presence of the other participant in a conversation. It concludes that different communication media result in varying psychological perceptions of presence cui_building_2013. For instance, mediums like videoconferencing offer a higher sense of social presence compared to e-mail. Giving the AI assistant a context-based personality and physical presence could enhance the visitors' perception of it. The holograms will be trained to be able to replicate human emotion and behavior leading to more engaging conversations. The social presence theory helps to understand the need for both physical and contextual parts in incorpating AI assistants in such an environment.

The methodology of this work combines qualitative observations, expert interviews, and technological prototype development.

First of all, a literature research will be conducted to identify existing ways of implementing needed functionalities. The focus will be the deployment of holograms in an open space, combining holograms with AI assistants and training large language models in a historical context. Also, it is important to understand the difficulties and capacities of each key objective. This helps both the holographic AI assistant's creator and the user to understand specific needs and challenges of its process and deployment (Sub-RQ1.1).

Additionally, expert interviews will be conducted to gain futher information about the integration requirements and specifically human interactions. Among these experts are three individuals who have experience with digital museum exhibits and six PhD students from Technische Universität Darmstadt which specialize in either machine learning and artificial intelligence or computer vision and human-computer interaction. The interview will be semi-structured combining open-ended and closed questions. This approach results in more flexibility in responses while still focusing on the specific areas of interest (Sub-RQ1.1 and Sub-RQ1.3).

Next, a small-scale prototype will be developed and evaluated. AI will rely on a pre-trained natural language model and training data will be sourced from publicly available historical papers and articles. The holographic rendering will take place in Unreal Engine, allowing for an adaptation into a physical holographic setup
girish_holographic_nodate (Sub-RQ1.1).

After that, a testing phase is crucial to gain feedback and evaluate the assistant's performance. Testing will take place in a controlled environment like a classroom in university and it will contain five to ten randomly selected participants who will simulate museum visitors. Each participant has the opportunity to interact with the holographic AI assistant for around ten to fifteen minutes, asking questions within the historical scope and playing different scenarios. The whole scene will be recorded and notes will be taken. The focus will be to evaluate the holographic AI assistant's natural behavior, the accuracy of its answers and its intuitiveness. After this, each participant will be asked to write down new insights they have gained and suggestions for improvement (Sub-RQ1.3).

It is especially important to bring our attention to ethical challenges and the use of faulty datasets that arise with the development and use of holographic AI assistants in museums. The main key that needs to be fulfilled is to guarantee historical accuracy and cultural awareness. This must be adhered to in order to ensure that no false or biased information is conveyed. Moreover, using AI to simulate historical figures raises ethical questions about representing deceased individuals, especially if their views are misrepresented. To address this, careful research comparing has to be conducted using academic databases. Furthermore, visitors' privacy must be guaranteed by ensuring that data generated during an interaction is anonymized with privacy measures like data anonymization and secure storage (Sub-RQ1.2).

Despite these risks, the combination of research interviews, development and user feedback allows for detailed evaluation of the usage of holographic AI assistants. Both technical and ethical requirements are considered, which is crucial to ensure that the system is not only functional but also culturally and morally responsible. This lays the foundation for future developments in the domain, promoting a responsible and effective integration of AI and holography in museums, enhancing interactive and immersive learning experiences for visitors.

This research is based on Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) theory, which defines the range between what a learner can do independently and what they can achieve with guidance website_def. The LLM-based teaching agent in this study will operationalize ZPD by continuously monitoring learner progress and adjusting the difficulty and nature of its responses accordingly. This will be achieved by analyzing student inputs, adapting explanations and challenges based on comprehension levels, and gradually reducing assistance as the learner gains confidence and proficiency. Approach

SOTA 

Neural rendering is a relatively new part of Computer graphics, but there has been immense progress in recent years Tewari2022. With many different ways in which it is used, from Neural Radiance Fields(NERFS) and Gaussian Splatting Qian2024 to more novel approaches such as Codec avatars from Meta Platforms, Inc.Shugao2021. In comparison, the development of classical human head rendering has been more gradual, with less big breakthroughs in the last couple of years. Instead, older techniques traditionally used in offline applications have been increasingly adopted in a real-time environment. 
A big example of this is ray tracing, which imitates real light by tracing rays through the scene. In recent years, it has been able to be displayed in many modern video games in real-timedeng2017toward, through the use of hardware acceleration.

It is customary that novel neural approaches are compared to their classical counterparts remondino2023critical, but there has been a lack of research comparing the different methods when it comes to photorealistic avatars. The comparisons that do exist are often secondary aspects of papers that primarily focus on introducing new techniques. 
This research aims to provide a broader perspective on the subject, with a bigger focus on the strengths and weaknesses of both approaches.



Theoretical Framework 

We have identified three different metrics, which are important to assess when choosing a rendering approach for realistic AI avatars. 

The first is efficiency, which evaluates the performance one can expect when implementing the given method. This is crucial for all real-time applications such as AI avatars, where rendering must occur within tight time constraints.

The second metric is realism. It describes how far away the resulting image is from a real picture of a person, a ground truth. I will use the Structural Similarity Index measure (SSIM)wang2004image, which measures how similar two images appear for humans, to get a more accurate evaluation.

The last one is adaptability, which assesses how easy it is to implement and adapt the given method. We will evaluate how much experience is necessary for the implementation of the technique and how easily it is adapted to ones needs.

Evaluating and comparing these metrics allows one to robustly compare the different approaches and draw an accurate conclusion on which methods work best for each use case.

Methodology 

The methodology will combine source research and quantitative methods.

The first step will be to extensively research, analyze and evaluate the most relevant papers on neural rendering and classical rendering relevant to photorealistic avatars. This means we will focus mainly on papers by computer graphics and AI researchers(our target group). Presentations by developers, held during conferences like the Game Developers Conference, will also be relevant. Once we have an overview, we can select comparable methods on both sides. This allows us to apply the theoretical framework to directly compare the approaches.

After having chosen the methods, we will start with the implementation. 
For the approaches where the creation is based on real pictures, we will use DSLR cameras to capture a high-quality scan of a fellow student's head. For the more manual methods, we will try to match the look of the head to the already scanned head.

During this phase, we will take note of any difficulties that arise and will take note of the time it takes to implement. This allows us to better judge the adaptability of each method.
To test efficiency we will benchmark each method on the Lichtenberg Cluster. This means we will request the Hochschulrechenzentrum(HRZ) of the TU Darmstadt for access. We will use the latency in milliseconds as a unit for measurement. 

After having gathered all the results in a single table in Microsoft Excel, we can move on to evaluate the realism. We will run the resulting image of each method through our implementation of the Structural Similarity Index measure in Python and compare each of them with a ground truth, which was already captured with the DSLR camera.
After this phase is over, we will go through each method and look at the efficiency, realism, and our notes on adaptability, which will allow us to then make a final evaluation and conclusion of each method.

In some neural rendering techniques like NeRFs gao2023nerf, only the creation of the scene involves a neural network. The actual rendering is done using traditional volume rendering techniques. 
This will make simple comparisons more difficult because we will also need to take the creation of the classical scene into account. This distinction needs to be made on a case-by-case basis for the most fair comparison.
Another problem is that the metrics laid out in the framework don't cover everything. An example of this is the amount of data required, which is typically a lot higher on the neural side. We will need to identify issues like these individually as well.

Thus, the theoretical framework should only be taken as a basis for the comparison. Because of this, the final assessment, while based on objective metrics, will be somewhat subjective.

Transforming Education: The Significance of Holographic AI Assistant in Education
Analysing How Holographic AI Technology Affects Student Engagement and Improve Participation
Caleb Diaz

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2924812                       
  




inf
Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing Lab










Motivation

More than 168 million students worldwide experienced disruptions in their education due to school closures resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic unicef2021covid. Consider a student in a far-off village who found it difficult to interact with the teacher using outdated and unreliable online sources. Imagine if the student had access to a holographic artificial intelligence (AI) assistant - a device that could provide realistic lessons to the learner in the comfort of their own home.

In the year 2000, a significant demonstration of holographic technology took place when a hologram of Catharine Darnton, a Math teacher was successfully beamed into an exhibition centre in a school in south London. While the distance of transition was relatively short, it proved that transmitting realistic images over the internet was feasible and recorded as an important milestone at the time aina2010application. Fast forward to today, advancements in holographic and artificial intelligence (AI) technology have brought us closer to integrating such innovations into everyday life, especially in education. The concept of enabling uninterrupted holographic lessons is no longer a far distant dream but a close reality, with the global AI in Education industry projected to surge from USD 3.79 Billion in 2022 to USD 20.54 Billion in 2027, with an extraordinary compund annual growth of 45.6\
\\

The main area of interest  resides at the junction of educational technology (ed-tech) and artificial intelligence (AI). Although tools such as AI-powered chatbots, virtual assistants have become popular, their capacity to match the depth and engagement of human teaching is still limited. These approaches encounter major obstacles to wider acceptance like engagement and flexibility.
With the growing costs of AI-tools like virtual reality (VR) accessibility is also an impactful matter in question. According to UNICEF report, at least 200 million school children live in 31 low-middle income countries that remained unprepared to deploy remote learning in future emergency school closures unicef2021least. This is where low hardware cost holographic AI could become a game changer also promoting a good internet connectivity which results in overall development and thus highlighting the critical demand for effective and accessible educational technologies. 
\\
Holographic AI assistant is a revolutionary solution to these challenges. By combining advanced holography and adaptive artificial intelligence (AI), the study aims to fill a critical gap in current educational practices and technologies, making education more accessible to all students.
    
Research question:\\
The main research question guiding this study is in what ways can holographic AI assistants improve participation, personalization and accessibility in education to create a better learning experience.                                                   In order to tackle this, this study investigates some extended questions-

     Which aspect of holographic AI most successfully boosts student engagement?
     In what ways can holographic AI provide personalised learning? 
     What are the opportunities and challenges with holographic AI assistant?
 



Approach
    Many educational institutions around the world are exploring technology as a means to enhance student engagement, improve learning outcomes, and promote equal access to resources. By combining the adaptability of artificial intelligence AI with the capabilities of holography, holographic AI assistants provide promising solutions to address these challenges.

SOTA - 



     AI-powered tools like learning management systems have highly improved the delivery of personalized educational content. For instance, Online-learning platforms use adaptive algorithms to customize learning pathways according to one's individual needs, thus making education more customised. However in distant or hybrid environments, these tools lack interaction and physical presence. As a result, such technologies regularly fail promoting dynamic interactions and emotional engagement of students Luckin2017.

     Taking into account the limits of existing AI tools, holography stands up as a promising option, with proven effective in specialised fields such as medical simulations. For example, holographic models of human ear anatomy have greatly improved experiential learning for medical students, offering a deeper level of understanding of the subject matter. gnanasegaram2020evaluating. Virtual reality (VR) aims to fulfill the requirements for physical presence and interactivity to mimic human educators, yet, its dependency on costly technology often makes it impractical for mass usage OECD2021. This situation highlights the need for a more cheap and scalable solution that combines best of both worlds, the interactivity of virtual reality (VR) and the adaptive intelligence of AI.


Theoretical Framework 




     Engagement Theory serves as a appropriate basis for this study. It focuses on the importance of meaningful activities and technological interaction in the learning process. It states that technology plays a crucial role in enhancing engagement by promoting active and genuine learning experiences kearsley1998engagement.

     Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge Theory (TPACK) follows a similar pattern. The TPACK theory combines technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge to improve educational outcomes. It offers a systematic method for the effective establishment of innovative technologies, including holographic AI, into teaching methodologies. This method supports the customisation of learning experiences to meet various student needs schad2021review.



Methodology 

To address the study’s research questions, a mixed methodological approach is used, which combines quantitative, and qualitative research to fully answer the research topics. This enables in-depth examination of the benefits, drawbacks, and difficulties of using holographic AI .

The study will collect both usability and engagement data on holographic AI through surveys and structured interviews. Specifically, quantitative data will measure interaction levels, perceived effectiveness, and ease of use, while qualitative data will explore students and teaching assistant perceptions, challenges, and potential improvements.

Given feasibility constraints, the study will focus on a smaller, manageable sample size, targeting approximately 50 students and 10 teaching assistants to ensure depth and practicality.

In order to gain a thorough understanding of contextual difficulties and user experiences, qualitative interviews will be put in practice. 10–15 semi-structured interviews will be conducted with educators to gather their views on challenges,  suggestions , perspectives and implementation concern on the use of holographic AI. 
Furthermore existing literature on holography will be reviewed in order to establish a strong theoretical basis for the study.


The target audience for this study comprises of students aged between 10 to 18. A secondary group includes Educators and school administrators, who are responsible for evaluating the usability, integration, and practicality of holographic AI tools in educational settings. Additionally, Ed-tech stakeholders, including developers play an important role in exploring the scalability and accessibility of these technologies.


Despite  its strengths such as the integration of theories from social presence , personalized education and constructivist learning, this study acknowledges the limitation of implementing holographic AI in underfunded schools that lack the necessary infrastructure.
However, a mixed-method approach ensures a thorough and delicate data collection process, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of the technology’s true potential.

Evaluating ”Do Not Provide Solution” Prompting for LLMs

Calvin Ferguson

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2565530                       
  




inf
Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing Lab










Motivation













Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT 4.0 have entered our classrooms, and it seems that they are here to stay. Some case studies already suggest that around 50\










Chatbot LLMs have only recently been widely adopted by the public, with ChatGPT surpassing 100 million users theverge_chatgpt_user_count_2023 in January 2023, two months after it became publicly available. These tools often provide appropriate answers and explanations to almost any natural language question asked. This has caused concern for many, who fear that our current methods of testing knowledge could be easily cheated, as these chatbots seem to offer a shortcut to many forms of graded written work. There are tools available that claim to detect the use of LLMs. However, their false positive rate is still too high to rely solely on their output elkhatat_evaluating_2023. On the other hand, the use of such tools can also have a positive learning effect, with many students reporting that it helps them to learn bernabei_students_2023. This suggests that an outright ban on the use of LLM tools in education may be the wrong approach. Instead, teachers and professors may need to adapt their teaching to include them in order to help students learn perkins_academic_2023. 

However, as LLMs are often used outside the control of any teacher supervision, students may be tempted to ask for solutions and only look at the steps provided or accept the answer as correct kazemitabaar_how_2023. Although examples and solutions can have a positive effect on learning, solving new problems independently is equally important for long-term learning atkinson_transitioning_2003. As this step can be time consuming and difficult, students may skip it if they have already found the solution they were looking for.



Considering this, it may be useful for LLMs to support students in finding solutions to problems without giving them the answer directly.  There is little or no prior evaluation of how willing these systems are to provide solutions when asked directly, and whether this has a negative impact on learning. On the other hand, if LLMs are capable enough to not give solutions, they could help to supplement teachers and provide individual help to students when no other help is available.









This study will focus on the following research questions:











     RQ1: How effectively can an LLM system be adapted to not providing solutions in any case, even if pressured on them? 
     RQ2: Do LLM assistants with a limited ability to provide solutions improve students learning?
    
         Sub-RQ2.1: Do students find these systems helpful, compared to other forms of teaching?
         Sub-RQ2.2: How frequent are occurrences of hallucinations and what impact do they have on learning?
    
     RQ3: How effective are current implementations of "teaching LLMs" at preventing cheating by students?


Approach













SOTA

The novelty of many publicly available LLM chatbots limits our knowledge, especially when it comes to using them in an educational context. There are different approaches that try to use LLMs to support student learning. One approach aims to simulate our current classroom interactions with multiple independent LLMs, each defined with a unique role or task zhang_simulating_2024. 

Other systems complement the classroom environment with LLM chatbots wang_chated_2023, neumann_llm-driven_2024 aimed at answering course-specific questions. 

Both approaches show good acceptance by students and offer opportunities to improve current teaching environments and students' learning of new concepts. However, both do not systematically address the issue of using the tools to cheat on graded submissions or to short-circuit the learning process. It is therefore possible that they are vulnerable to such attempts by students. 

There is an evaluation of different types of guidance that students receive for their use of LLMs kumar_impact_2024. They also compare a prompted LLM with one that did not receive a prompt. Although this prompt includes the instruction not to provide solutions, it is not tested for its effectiveness. Interestingly, the study finds no significant change in performance when comparing the prompted and unprompted agents. Evaluating the effectiveness of prompts that prohibit LLMs from providing solutions may help to understand how prompts can affect learning.















Theoretical Framework

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable abilities in various NLP tasks. They are trained on massive amounts of data, often large parts of the Internet, and are able to generate human-like responses to natural language input with a quality that can rival human responses koubaa_exploring_2023. This study will use existing and proven LLM chatbots for evaluation, as the training of LLM chatbots can be very time consuming. 

The quality of LLM responses often depends on the use of specific prompting techniques liu_prompting_2023. In this technique, trained LLMs are provided with specific inputs to guide them in generating the desired output. In addition, LLMs can be aligned during training to guide their output in a desired direction wang_comprehensive_2024. This process of training a model to give preferred answers cannot be done without direct access to the model. This study aims to evaluate existing chat interfaces such as ChatGPT. For this reason, only prompting is used. 

Both prompting and alignment are used to limit the output of LLMs to prevent harmful or otherwise unwanted output. However, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where specific user input bypasses the guidelines wei_jailbroken_2023. These bypasses could allow students to access solutions when they should not.

Another common problem with LLMs is hallucinations, answers invented by LLMs that are factually incorrect but look legitimate huang_survey_2024. Hallucinations can occur especially when there is insufficient or poor quality data on a topic perkovic_hallucinations_2024. Such answers can potentially have a very negative impact on learning, as students may still accept the given solution as correct, sometimes actively damaging what a student already knows. 

Students will be guided in their use of the LLM tools. Kumar et al. show that guidance such as providing students with a list of suggestions for using the tools, giving examples of instructions they could give, or asking metacognitive questions can help improve students' use of these tools kumar_impact_2024. 

Methodology


This study will evaluate the publicly available LLM chatbot GPT 4.0. It is chosen based on its popularity especially amongst students.

Additionally, a combination of LLMs following the prompts and roles of zhang_simulating_2024 will be recreated. 

To evaluate the prompting in a first step, a qualitative study will test the LLMs with predefined queries to see if they provide learning steps but not complete solutions in different scenarios. Several prompting techniques will be evaluated liu_prompting_2023. The prompts will be tested for resistance to jailbreaking, using common methods to try to bypass restrictions. This study may also be repeated to fine-tune the prompting used to limit the output of LLMs. Data will be collected on the final effectiveness of the prompts in the scenarios by answering RQ1.

A quantitative study will then be carried out on computer science students. This target population is chosen so that all participants are familiar and experienced in learning new topics efficiently. The participants will be split into multiple groups. Specifically, two groups will have access to an LLM assistant with or without specific prompting. In an adjacent experiment, a group of students will be given access to the simulated classroom. These groups are given guidance in the form of general instructions about the LLM and some examples of questions they might ask. They are not instructed on whether or not they can or should ask for the solution directly. In addition, a control group will learn about the topic through conventional means, i.e. textbooks. The students are then asked to answer questions about a topic in a domain new to them, using the tools available to them to learn about the topic. 

All groups will then be asked new questions to test their understanding and answer Sub-RQ2. In addition, they will be asked for their subjective opinion on the trust they have in these systems and the perceived helpfulness. This will help to answer Sub-RQ2.1. The group using the simulated classroom will be monitored for incidents of cheating to answer RQ3.

The quantitative study will involve a minimum of 20 participants, each of whom will complete the study individually in a controlled environment with restricted access only to the tested LLM assistant. Each group will have a minimum of 5 participants.

An analysis will be carried out to check for hallucinated answers that LLMs might provide. It can then be analysed what effect these hallucinations had to answer Sub-RQ3. 

Some students may also try to jailbreak the restrictions to avoid the assessment. Occurrences of this will also be analysed and excluded from the data, if the students succeed. If these occurrences are frequent, they may indicate an inherent weakness in this teaching approach.

This main analysis should provide an insight into the learning effect that different LLM tools can help with. As each group consists of 5 people, it should be possible to include the variance for each tool. At the very least, it should provide a good comparison of using LLMs to learn about a topic versus the control group using only textbooks.

The Role of Visual Representation in Shaping Trust and Usability in AI Assistants


Cassandra Blankenship

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2308577

Motivation
Adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has reached a tipping point across domains. In many scientific endeavours AI is now a core part, like in natural language processing or computer vision. This, however, cannot be said for user-focused applications. While AI certainly gained in popularity through ChatGPT, Midjourney and the like, AI-based chatbots still frequently fail to meet customer expectations AI-based_chatbots_in_customer_service_and_their_effects_on_user_compliance and AI assistants often can't shake the connection to their impersonal, dry and quite frankly gimmicky predecessors like Alexa and Siri. All this in spite of the massive improvements that the field of AI has seen in the last decade, especially with Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 or Claude A_Survey_of_Large_Language_Models. \\
So the question now becomes, how does one realign the user perception with the actual power of these systems?

The most promising approach to raise perceived capabilities, that isn't improving the AI model outright, has been anthropomorphising AI systems. Giving AI traits usually associated with humans increases trust and loyalty towards them Virtual_Customer_Service_Agents:_Using_Social_Presence_and_Personalization_to_Shape_Online_Service_Encounters. This is already being done in many ways, for example Alexa and Siri both have a female voice and name. \\
While human voices as well as avatar pictures do increase perceived sociability Virtual_Customer_Service_Agents:_Using_Social_Presence_and_Personalization_to_Shape_Online_Service_Encounters, the next step forward is for our virtual assistants to come to life through holographic projections. 


This study will focus on this aforementioned gap by posing the following research questions:

    [Research Question 1:] How much does providing an anthropomorphic visual representation improve the perceived capabilities of an AI system?


    [] RQ1.1: How do augmented, virtual, and mixed reality compare to simple picture avatars, in regards to fostering social presence? 
    [] RQ1.2: How does the level of realism impact this perception?


Approach
In the last decades there has been a massive increase in scientific as well as commercial incentives to design social conversational agents (CAs)
Towards_Designing_Cooperative_and_Social_Conversational_Agents_for_Customer_Service. This can decrease cost while providing better and more personalized services. Actors that have greater social presence are also linked with greater customer satisfaction Virtual_Customer_Service_Agents:_Using_Social_Presence_and_Personalization_to_Shape_Online_Service_Encounters. If further benefits can be gained by moving away from simple avatars to three dimensional projections is unclear.  

The demand for conversational agents is not limited to working with customers. The educational sector has long been experimenting with AI assistants. Be it in museums or classrooms, chatbots have seen a general increase in e-learning applications Self-regulated_learning_with_approximate_reasoning_and_situation_awareness. In this use AI assistants create an interactive learning experience and take on the role of a one-to-one interaction with a teacher Chatbot:_An_Education_Support_System_for_Student. In such a context the social connection one feels has a crucial impact on learning speed and motivation. It is, however, unclear if text alone or simple pictures on displays suffice to create such a social connection. 

The before mentioned research rarely exceeds a simple 2D avatar. So the question now becomes, does this trend of  more human like characteristics leading to a better response in users continue into the third dimension?

In museums and cultural heritage sites there have already been successfully combinations of both chatbots and holographic displaysA_Survey_of_Augmented_Virtual_and_Mixed_Reality_for_Cultural_Heritage. When integrated into their pedagogy, it has been shown that augmented and mixed reality can enhance the sense of presence as well as aid in the learning process Discovering_Leonardo_with_artificial_intelligence_and_holograms:_A_user_study.

When considering which technology to choose, the perceived capabilities may also depend on the type of problem that is to be solved. In the context of more educationally focused uses, different technologies are usually chosen dependent on the use case A_Survey_of_Augmented_Virtual_and_Mixed_Reality_for_Cultural_Heritage.
This is important as it is likely that the perceived capabilities may also depend on the fit of the AI system to the problem that is being solved.



The technologies to facilitate this kind of social conversational agent fall into three main categories:

    [Virtual Reality:] Virtual Reality (VR) systems like the Meta Quest completely replace ones vision with a virtual rendering, allowing for immersion and versatility.  
    [Augmented and Mixed Reality:] Augmented and mixed reality systems like the Microsoft HoloLens enrich your view of the real world with digital assets. Where augmented reality (AR) mostly uses visuals overlays that are fixed to screen space, mixed reality often uses tracking to place objects into the world.
    [Stationary Projections:] Stationary Projections use techniques like pepper ghost pyramid projection to project a 3D image in real life. This has the advantage of removing the need for clunky headsets or glasses, but usually confine the 3D model to a single spot or room.


This paper will mostly focus on the first two categories, as they are more suited for AI assistants. This is because personal assistants, as we use them today, need to be accessible at all times and therefore rely on portability.
Because of this, wearable solutions are preferred for AI assistants

The paper will guide itself along the theoretical concepts of:

    [Social Presence Theory:] Social Presence Theory suggests that communication mediums vary in how much they allow people to feel present with each other. Nonverbal cues like facial expressions, eye contact, and body language enhance this "social presence," making interactions feel more immediate and engaging social_presence_theory.
    [Embodied Cognition Theory:] The theory of embodied cognition suggests that the body functions (especially in context of our senses) are a constituent of the mind rather than a perceiver and actor serving the mind embodied_cognition. This theory ties in with the theory of social presence and can help explain how physical interactions, both with and by an artificial assistant, can help with user engagement.




To help understand how much the presentation impacts the perceived capabilities of an AI system (RQ1), a participants study will be conducted. In this study users will be given a task, that is to be solved with the help of an AI system. The task will be randomly chosen out of a pool of tasks, that represent everyday problems, like knowledge acquisition. The users will interact with the same underlying AI system using different representations to solve these tasks. The participants of the study will be of mixed age, gender and social background. This is important, as the domain of holographic AI assistants encompasses anywhere from schools to home assistants. 
\\
The different representations will range from only using text or audio, to using avatars in form of pictures up to 3D holographic avatars and spanning both VR and AR (RQ1.1 \& RQ1.2). The visualisation as well as task will be randomized, all while using the same underlying LLM to isolate the impact of the different representations.\\ 
The study will be conducted as a blind experiment, meaning the participants won't know the actual research questions before they give their answers.

To evaluate the experiment, the users will rate their experiences for each of the different AI systems. On top of that they will also give feedback in form of a short interview, to gain both quantitative and qualitative data.

It has been shownDevelopment_of_Human-Computer_Interaction_for_Holographic_Ais that previous experience with AR, or systems like it, can increase the adoption speed and impact the baseline attitude towards such systems. Because of this, the survey will also contain a section to evaluate the participants prior interaction with systems like Augmented and Virtual Reality as well as AI in general. This will try to minimize the effect of bias for or against AI assistants, but it will not be possible to remove it entirely.\\
Another limitation will be the avatars used for the advanced AI visualisations, as these technologies are still being developed and are therefore hard to get a hold of. To limit the scope of the project, an already existing LLM with an additional visual representation will be used, instead of a new custom built AI model.

Effective Personalized Learning With Large Language Models
Improving Intent Selection of the Stratl Algorithm with Artificial Intelligence Methods
Charles Grimes

Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych           
Dennis Zyska                 
2314406                       
  




inf
Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing Lab










Motivation

Effective tutoring is characterized by the so-called "2 Sigma Problem"~bloom19842. This problem is described by Bloom, who found that the average student performs about two standard deviations better when being tutored one-to-one, in contrast to conventional methods~bloom19842. Obviously, pairing each student worldwide with a one-to-one teacher is not feasible. A classroom in public schools normally consists of a teacher and more than 20 students. Creating personalized learning paths for all students is a very difficult task for teachers. Furthermore, learners benefit greatly from feedback on their work~Schartel_2012. Again, teachers do not have the time to provide feedback on every exercise a student performs.\\
State-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) can solve questions in several subjects~wang2024largelanguagemodelseducation and achieve scores similar to those of students on standardized tests~openai2023gpt. Using them as tutors would offer a solution to the 2 Sigma Problem. However, they are trained with human feedback~ouyang2022training, humans normally prefer fast answers to their queries. This is counterproductive to the object of learning. \\
For education, LLMs should be adjusted so that they do not give the answer directly, but rather help students find it themselves. The conservative approach to tutoring is called "Direct Instruction"~adams2003direct. In contrast, Kapur~kapur2008productive suggests that maximum learning is achieved by Productive Failure (PF). PF describes confronting learners with the problem first, letting them try finding a solution themselves. Only afterwards are they presented with the possible solution.\\
Implementing PF into a LLM tutor should be the objective. A LLM tutor would be accessible to nearly every student. So it could leverage the positive effects of one-to-one tutoring and offer personalization. Combined with the maximized learning from PF, it would optimize learning to a great extend. Puech et. al. attempted to do exactly this and developed "StratL", an algorithm to strategically prompt a LLM~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. This algorithm classifies the current state of the student. Based on this classification it chooses a tutor intent from a transition graph. This way, the prompted LLM can give hints personalized for the user. This personalization follows the goal of maximum learning in a PF manner~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. StratL showed promising results in terms of students producing Representation and Solution Methods (RSMs). Still, there is room for improvement, as reports of the field study suggest suboptimal classification at times~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. Intent selection is the key to a PF-based LLM-tutor.\\
In the proposed thesis, the following research question is going to be addressed:

RQ: How can the classification of the students state of the StratL algorithm be improved?\\
{}

     sub RQ1: Can a k-Nearest-Neighbor approach improve the StratL classification algorithm?
     sub RQ2: Can a Decision Tree improve the StratL classification algorithm?
     sub RQ3: Can a fine-tuned LLM improve the StratL classification algorithm?
 


Approach

State of the Art\\
Wang et. al. describe the current state of LLMs in education~wang2024largelanguagemodelseducation. They write about the nearly perfect ability of LLMs to solve questions~openai2023gpt. Other areas, such as error correction, content generation and giving feedback are very advanced as well. In Knowledge Tracing, that is tracking a learners understanding, there are also active developments being made~wang2024largelanguagemodelseducation. LLMs are now able to predict a students' answer based on their knowledge profiles~wang2024largelanguagemodelseducation. The application of LLMs as Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) are explored. A thorough review of the literature revealed no further work on the implementation of PF into LLMs other than the paper on StratL~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. \\
Integrating Artificial Intelligence into education is an objective nearly everyone agrees on. That is always paired with the fear of raising plagiarism. Most work~wang2024largelanguagemodelseducation in this area is based on the problem of how to tune LLMs to switch from answering questions to being an effective tutor. Answering questions raises plagiarism concerns, while an effective tutor supports students in finding the answer themselves. 

This thesis work is going to further investigate if the StratL Algorithm~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage can provide a solution to this. Right now, it successfully makes students produce RSMs, which can be seen as a metric for how well it follows the PF approach. However, there are deficits in terms of the classification of the students state. This state is essential, as it forms the basis for selecting the agent’s intent. If students are misunderstood, the agent tries to help them with problems they do not even have. Puech et. al.~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage managed to develop an agent that gives answers in a PF manner. If this agent further achieves to classify all its users correctly, it will be the most efficient learning tool.

Theoretical Framework\\
The more conservative approach to learning is called {Direct Instruction} (DI)~adams2003direct. In this approach, teachers show students a way to tackle a specific problem, going through every necessary step to find the solution. Afterwards, the students are presented problems of the same type. They are expected to solve them using the same steps they were presented beforehand. \\
In order to help students gain maximum knowledge, the concept of {Productive Failure} (PF) plays a key role~kapur2008productive. Learning has shown to be more effective when students are not directly presented with the solution. Confronting students with the problem first, without showing them how to solve it is beneficial. Before revealing the possible solution, they try to find their own way. That is known as PF~kapur2008productive. The aim of this approach is not that students find the right way to the solution themselves, but rather that they fail in the first place. This way, learning is maximized when they are presented with the solution afterwards. It is proven to be superior to DI in terms of learning effects. \\
{StratL} is an algorithm introduced by Puech et. al.~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage that tries to implement PF into a LLM tutor. To what extend the tutor accomplishes this is measured by the number of {Representation and Solution Methods} (RSMs) produced by its student. These RSMs can be seen as partial solutions that the students came up with. They motivate further search for the solution and thereby display participation in PF. Furthermore, a {PF score} is used for evaluation. This PF score is higher if the students find more predefined crucial reasoning steps themselves, which can be associated with their learning. The algorithm returns a student state, that is further used to prompt a LLM. Previously, the same LLM has been prompted with initial PF instructions that for example prohibit giving the answer directly. \\
Deciding on the current state of the student is integral to the effectiveness of tutoring. Providing students with hints that asked for a definition does not enhance their learning or worse, makes them lose confidence in the abilities of the tutor. At the moment, there is no Artificial Intelligence (AI) being used when it comes to the student state tracing in StratL. AI is still an integral part of the tutor as a LLM is prompted in the end. When a field study was run, participants reported problems. Particularly, they described that answers of the tutor did not match their query.
It is investigated whether it is possible to reach a better classification with machine learning techniques. There is a dataset provided by the developers of StratL. This dataset can be used to evaluate the performance of an altered version in terms of how good it follows PF.

Methodology\\
To enhance the StratL algorithm, access to its source code is required. Fortunately, it is available as open-source software~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. The same holds for the dataset~puech2024pedagogicalsteeringlargelanguage. This dataset consists of 20 unique problems that require multiple interactions to be solved. Based on these problems, a tutor with a changed StratL algorithm can be evaluated. For evaluation, the rubrics of RSMs and PF score can be used. Students can be simulated with GPT-4. This quantitative approach can be a foundation for further studies. It is to be noted that both of the scores have to be counted manually, which can be time-intensive. Still, this approach is useful as changes can be made and tested simultaneously. The changes themselves will be made using the Hugging Face and PyTorch frameworks. For sub RQ1 and sub RQ2, I will adjust the hyperparameters. Comparing with the results the simulated student and the dataset problems deliver, these will be adjusted more coarse- or fine-grained. To answer sub RQ3, I aim to leverage Low-Rank Adaptation~hu2021lora in order to fine-tune a LLM. The schedule for finding a good solution is the same as for the other parts, although this will probably take more time. Additionally, the resulting algorithm has to be checked in terms of running time. If it manages to classify the students state better, but takes too much time it might be more feasible to use a different approach. Too much time in this context refers to the resulting answer time the whole system needs or the training time.\\
In order to really address the potential improvements real-world studies have to be done. The classification problems of StratL only became clear with real students in the first place. Ideally, a group of students is recruited that participates in quantitative as well as qualitative studies. Quantitive in a sense that the interactions are evaluated based on the same metrics used with the simulated student interactions. Qualitative here means interviews on overall experience with emphasis on how well they felt understood by the tutor. The qualitative methods should be prioritized, as they more directly address the classification problem. These students can be of any school age, as PF applies across all domains. 

Difficulties\\
There are some problems that could occur during the implementation of these ideas. First, there could be problems with the code. For example, it could not be complete or the dataset could be too small. As the authors actively promote the idea of others further working with their open source work, these are considered unlikely. As for the dataset, there would have to be more examples produced, which could be done in buffer time. \\
The next problem could emerge if no students are found for the study. I still keep good relations with many of my school teachers and work at an elementary school, so I hope to find participants there. As I work as a tutor myself, I could also do the study on my tutor students. \\
For the qualitative method, there is to be considered that students mistake the answers of the LLM tutor as not fitting to their intent. If one is not familiar with PF or awaits a quick answer to the question, the answers in PF manner can cause frustration. This frustration could lead one to the conclusion that the tutor wrongly classifies. However, this can be intercepted and a precise questionnaire can bring differentiation.
